description: The major religious roles open to women — priestesses, the Pythia, Vestal Virgins and women-only festivals.
content_html:
A Rare Path to Public Life

In ancient Athens and Rome, women were largely excluded from civic and political life. Yet religion offered something different: roles of genuine authority and public visibility that few other spheres of society permitted. A priestess could own property in trust for a deity, lead public ceremonies attended by thousands, and earn the kind of respect usually reserved for men. Understanding these religious roles is essential for evaluating just how restricted—or unexpectedly empowered—women were in the classical world.

Greek Priestesses and Prophetesses

Greek sanctuaries regularly appointed women to serve female deities, and sometimes male ones too. The hiereia (priestess) held a position of real status. The most famous religious role open to a woman in all the ancient world was that of the Pythia, the oracle at Delphi. A woman, believed to be inspired directly by the god Apollo, sat on a tripod above a crack in the earth inside the inner sanctuary of the Temple of Apollo. Suppliants from across the Greek world — individuals, cities and kings — paid substantial fees to consult her, and her pronouncements could shape military campaigns and political decisions. The power she wielded, though in the name of a god, was genuinely extraordinary.

The literary source Plutarch, writing in his essay On the Oracles at Delphi, describes the process in some detail. A suppliant would purify himself, offer a goat sacrifice, pay the consultation fee, and then put his question to the male priests who passed it on to the Pythia in her inner chamber. Her response, often ambiguous, was delivered in prose or verse and interpreted by the priests. Plutarch was writing in the Roman period, long after the height of the oracle’s influence, but his account helps us picture how the consultation worked. The Pythia herself remained anonymous — we know no individual Pythia by name from the classical period — which tells us something important: her power came from the god, not from her personal identity.

Key Fact

The Pythia was the prophetess of Apollo at Delphi. She was a woman (usually an older woman taken from ordinary life) who delivered divine pronouncements to suppliants from across the Greek world. Her role gave women unparalleled spiritual authority in the Greek world.

Women’s Roles in Greek Festivals

Several major Athenian festivals required female participants. The Thesmophoria was one of the most widespread festivals in the Greek world, celebrated by citizen women across Athens and many other city-states. For five days each autumn (the Athenian Thesmophoria lasted five days in Attica, though only three days in much of the rest of the Greek world), citizen women left their households, set up camps near a sanctuary, and performed secret rites connected to the fertility of the earth and the myth of Persephone’s descent to the underworld. Men were completely excluded. The festival required women to take on significant organisational roles: the wealthiest women funded the ritual costs, and others carried out the ceremonial acts. The Thesmophoria demonstrates that certain religious spaces belonged entirely to women.

The Great Panathenaia was a very different festival. Here women participated prominently alongside men in a great civic procession along the Sacred Way to the Acropolis. The Parthenon Frieze — a continuous carved marble relief running around all four sides of the outer wall of the temple, now largely in the British Museum — appears to depict elements of the Panathenaic procession. Women and girls are carved in the frieze presenting offerings and walking in stately procession. Whether the frieze shows mortals or heroised figures is debated by scholars, but it places women at the visual and religious heart of the city’s most important civic celebration.

In ancient Athens, women played the central role in preparing the bodies of the dead and leading lamentation. The ritual of prothesis (laying out the corpse) was performed entirely by women. They washed the body, anointed it with oil, wrapped it in grave clothes, and led the communal mourning. Female mourning was considered both a religious duty and an expression of proper piety. However, Athenian law codes in the fifth century BC attempted to restrict female lamentation in public as being too emotionally excessive. The fact that legislation tried to curb it suggests how powerful and public women’s religious mourning actually was.

Roman Priestesses: The Vestal Virgins

Rome’s most prominent female religious institution was the college of Vestal Virgins. There were six Vestals at any time, each serving for thirty years: ten years of training, ten years of active service, and ten years of teaching new initiates. They were recruited between the ages of six and ten from respectable Roman families. Their central duty was to tend the sacred flame of Vesta in her circular temple in the Roman Forum. The flame represented Rome’s vitality; if it went out, disaster for the city was feared.

The legal position of the Vestal Virgins was extraordinary for Roman women. Normally, a Roman woman was under the legal authority of a male guardian (paterfamilias or tutor). The Vestals were freed from this authority: they could make wills, own property, give testimony in court without taking an oath, and travel through the city in a special carriage. They were accorded seats of honour at public games. If a Vestal passed a condemned criminal on the way to execution, he was automatically pardoned. This combination of purity requirements with extraordinary legal privilege marks the Vestals as unique in the Roman world. In exchange, the requirement of chastity was absolute: a Vestal found guilty of breaking her vow was buried alive in a small underground chamber sealed with earth.

Key Fact

The Vestal Virgins held unique legal privileges: they were freed from the authority of a male guardian, could make wills, own property, and give testimony in court. A condemned man they passed received an automatic pardon. The penalty for breaking their vow of chastity was to be buried alive.

Other Roman Religious Roles for Women

Alongside the Vestals, Rome had other female priestly roles. The Flaminica Dialis was the wife of Rome’s high priest of Jupiter. She was not simply a supporting spouse: her own purity and ritual behaviour were as strictly regulated as her husband’s, and she shared the burden of numerous taboos. Roman women also participated in the worship of the Bona Dea (Good Goddess), whose annual December rite was conducted entirely by women in the house of a senior magistrate. Men were forbidden from even knowing the details of the ceremony. Cicero’s speeches describe the scandal caused by Publius Clodius Pulcher, who disguised himself as a woman to infiltrate the ceremony in 62 BC.

Rome also had a tradition of the Sibyl, a prophetess whose oracular books were consulted by the Roman Senate in times of crisis. The most famous was the Cumaean Sibyl near Naples. These prophetesses, like the Pythia, exercised their authority through divine inspiration rather than civic office — but the effect was the same: a woman whose words could redirect the course of Roman policy.

Both Greek and Roman religion gave women formal roles that granted public visibility and status unmatched in other areas of life. Greek priestesses served a wide range of deities; Roman religion created a more structured institution in the Vestals. Both cultures had female prophetesses (Pythia / Sibyl) whose authority came from divine inspiration. A key difference is that the Vestals also had legal privileges that extended well beyond the religious sphere, suggesting Rome went further in recognising women’s religious service with tangible civic rewards. In Greece, the Pythia’s power remained strictly religious and her personal identity was submerged in the god’s. The material source, the Parthenon Frieze, shows Greek women in a communal, ordered procession; the round Temple of Vesta in the Roman Forum, with its sacred flame maintained only by women, makes a very different visual statement about female religious authority as the beating heart of the Roman state itself.
exam_tip_html: When a question uses the command word ‘Describe’ for a priestess or festival, give at least three factual details: what the person or festival was, where it took place, and what specific role women played. The examiner rewards precise knowledge. When the question asks you to ‘Explain’ or ‘Analyse’ a source, resist simply narrating what it shows — push to say what it reveals about the status of women or the culture’s values. The most common error in essays on women and religion is over-generalising: students write “women had no power” when the evidence of the Vestals and the Pythia shows the opposite. Use named sources (Parthenon Frieze, the Vestal’s House, Plutarch) to support every claim.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Religion was one of the few spheres of ancient life where women held formal, publicly recognised authority — as priestesses, prophetesses, and festival organisers in both Greece and Rome.
  • The Pythia at Delphi and the Vestal Virgins at Rome are the most prominent examples: both gave women extraordinary influence (political through the Pythia, legal through the Vestals) that went well beyond their usual domestic sphere.
  • Women-only festivals such as the Thesmophoria and the Bona Dea rites show that certain sacred spaces belonged exclusively to women, suggesting religion offered a genuine, if bounded, alternative public identity.

practice_questions.text: Name the prophetess who delivered Apollo's oracle at Delphi.
Describe the role and duties of the Vestal Virgins at Rome.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any three of: they tended the sacred flame of Vesta in her temple in the Roman Forum; they served for thirty years (ten training, ten active, ten teaching); they were recruited between the ages of six and ten from good families; they were freed from the authority of a male guardian; they could make wills and own property; a Vestal found guilty of breaking her vow of chastity was buried alive.

practice_questions.text:
Read the following passage, which paraphrases a description of the Thesmophoria festival:

'For five days each autumn, the women of Athens left their homes and set up camps near a sanctuary. No man was permitted to enter. The women who could afford it paid for the animals to be sacrificed; others carried out the sacred rites connected with the earth and with the story of Persephone. The festival had to be organised and funded by the women themselves.'

What does this passage reveal about the religious roles available to Athenian women? Use details from the passage in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A thorough analysis that uses multiple specific details from the passage (e.g. the exclusion of men, the women's organisational and funding roles, the connection to Persephone's myth) and links them to the broader significance of the Thesmophoria as evidence that women had real religious agency and a sacred sphere entirely their own. Draws a supported judgement, perhaps noting the paradox of public religious authority alongside domestic confinement.
Secure: Uses at least two details from the passage and explains what each reveals about women's religious roles. Makes a clear point about what this shows, such as that women could exercise genuine authority and initiative in a religious context.
Developing: Identifies one or two details from the passage and makes a basic observation about women's religious life, but the explanation of significance is limited or undeveloped.
Emerging: Mentions the passage in a general way without specific detail or explains it very briefly without engaging with significance.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the role of the Pythia was significant for our understanding of the status of women in the ancient Greek world.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying who the Pythia was (the prophetess of Apollo at Delphi). 1 mark for explaining what made her role significant (she influenced political decisions and military campaigns; rulers and city-states consulted her). 1 mark for contextualising this against the normal position of women (Athenian women were typically confined to the home and excluded from public life). 1 mark for a supporting detail (e.g. her identity was submerged in the god, suggesting her authority came from divine inspiration rather than personal status; she was drawn from ordinary women).

practice_questions.text: How far do the religious roles of women in Greece and Rome suggest that women had real power in the ancient world? Use a range of named sources in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained, well-structured argument that engages with the key tension: religious roles gave women real authority and public visibility, but this power was bounded, conditional, and defined by purity. Uses named sources from both cultures (Pythia, Thesmophoria, Parthenon Frieze for Greece; Vestal Virgins, Bona Dea rites, Temple of Vesta, Flaminica Dialis for Rome). Compares the two cultures fairly, noting that the Vestals' legal privileges went beyond Greece in giving women tangible civic rights. Reaches a supported judgement: religion gave women genuine power in specific, defined spheres, but this was not the same as equality with men.
Secure: Discusses examples from both cultures with relevant source references and makes a clear argument about the degree of power women held. Sustains an explanation throughout and offers a conclusion, even if not fully nuanced.
Developing: Covers some relevant material from one or both cultures but the argument is uneven. Sources may be named but not fully analysed. The conclusion may be asserted rather than argued.
Emerging: Makes general points about women and religion, possibly listing some roles without explaining their significance or using named sources consistently.

practice_questions.text: How similar were the religious roles available to women in Greece and Rome? Give at least two examples from each culture in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced comparison that identifies both similarities (both cultures had formal female priesthoods, both had female prophetesses whose words shaped state decisions, both had women-only sacred rites) and genuine differences (Vestals had legal privileges beyond the religious sphere; Greek ritual mourning and the Thesmophoria gave women control over important communal rites). Uses named examples from each culture (Pythia, hiereia, Thesmophoria for Greece; Vestal Virgins, Bona Dea, Sibyls, Flaminica Dialis for Rome). Reaches a supported conclusion.
Secure: Gives two clear examples from each culture, identifies at least one similarity and one difference, and supports with named evidence.
Developing: Gives examples from both cultures but the comparison is limited; similarities or differences may be implied rather than stated directly.
Emerging: Covers one culture in more detail than the other, or lists roles without comparing them.

glossary_terms.definition: A woman appointed to perform rituals on behalf of a deity, managing a temple's worship and rites.
The Greek term for a priestess, a woman appointed to serve a particular deity and carry out cult activities.
The prophetess at Delphi who sat on a tripod over a chasm and delivered the pronouncements of Apollo.

A women-only fertility festival held in Athens and across the Greek world in honour of Demeter and Persephone, from which men were excluded. In Athens (Attica) the festival lasted five days; elsewhere in the Greek world it typically lasted three days.
A great civic and religious festival held at Athens every four years in honour of Athena, featuring a procession, contests, and the presentation of a new robe to the goddess.
The Greek ritual laying out of a corpse for mourning, carried out by the women of the household before the funeral procession.
Six women at Rome who served the goddess Vesta by maintaining the sacred flame and received extraordinary legal privileges in return for a thirty-year vow of chastity.
The wife of the Flamen Dialis (high priest of Jupiter at Rome), who shared in her husband's religious duties and was subject to her own strict ritual regulations.
A Roman goddess of good women, worshipped exclusively by women in rites from which men were strictly excluded.
A female prophet in the Roman world; the Cumaean Sibyl's oracular books were consulted by the Roman Senate in times of national crisis.
